11:14 EDT deleted the family's key and minted another, while the custody sealed at the first stayed; the last run
committed the receipt of a key whose password nobody sealed, and Keycloak held the password of a key deleted hours
earlier (SES: `535 Authentication Credentials Invalid`). The AWS-admin recovery assumed the phases that continue a dead
attempt carry no target receipt; the retained lane writes its Target before the journal commits one, and the execution
algebra committed whatever receipt it observed. It now adopts an observed Target only for an initial attempt resumed
by its own permit; a freshly minted key, and any remint, runs the bounded cleanup and refuses by name
(`recovery-remint-ambiguous/target-holds-predecessor-material`), leaving no key behind and writing nothing over the
Target. Four new cases drive the production algebra over a scripted journal, IAM inventory and Target (red on the old
line: `got: Right ()`), and canonical `prodbox dev check` exits 0 (primary unit **5,599/5,599**). **Live proof: none
to give**: the window needs a process death between a delivery and its commit, which no suite produces. Adopting the
dead attempt's key instead of refusing is not built, and the block says so; Sprint `8.13`'s scope revision is the
rotation a refused family takes. **Deployment qualification: pending** under Standard P (invalidated: the AWS-admin
worker's recovery changed).

**Sprint `5.53` is Active (2026-10-15): four more deliverables landed code-locally.** The retained-volume ensure
refuses a listed volume smaller than the plan, or one that reports no size, naming the volume and both sizes and
before it creates anything for the others (the conservative arm of the operator decision; growing in place is not
built); the cleanup client's suite id is substrate-scoped, so a live run one substrate left is not adopted by the
other (`all` was `all` on both); and the harness submits its ACME EAB fixture under an operation id that carries a
digest of the credential frame, where it was the cluster alone, so a changed `acme_eab` is installed as a rotation
at the next generation instead of replaying the retained one; and the Provider's EBS, Route 53 validation-zone and
owned-tag interpreters, which started their own unbounded `aws` process, now take the runner as an argument and the
Provider passes its bounded, permit-serialised one. Nine new cases, three of them shown red by a mutation exercise
that removed each check in turn (the volume size check twice and the suite id), and canonical `prodbox dev check`
exits 0 (primary unit
**5,608/5,608**). The rest of the sprint is listed in its block. **Live proof: pending**; nothing here can be proven
without a live account, the EAB case needs a changed `acme_eab`, and the Provider changes reach a cluster only with
the next runtime image.

**Sprint `5.57` is Done (2026-10-15): the DNS validation waits for the Gateway-DNS write authority.** The final
regression sweep ran `public-dns` right after `aws-iam` and `dns-aws` and it failed in two minutes with `Gateway-DNS
observation is bound to the requested record but its write authority is not ready`; `dns check` answered the same for a
few minutes and then `in-sync`. Only the gateway node that holds the ownership claim reports it can write, the state is
served by whichever node the loopback endpoint reaches, and each gateway Pod restarts about every ninety minutes. The
public-edge wait already retries exactly this refusal; the validation read it once. It now retries it up to thirty
times ten seconds apart and ends the wait at once on anything else; three new cases, and canonical `prodbox dev check`
exits 0 (primary unit **5,595/5,595**). **Live proof: observed 2026-10-15** — `public-dns` passed the Route 53 and
resolver checks right after `dns-aws` and failed only at the HTTP redirect while the `lifecycle` suite's rebuild had left
no Gateway, then passed in full once `charts reconcile vscode` restored the edge; the validation is silent when the wait
absorbs a refusal, so the three scripted cases remain the proof of the absorbing path. **Deployment qualification:
pending** under Standard P (not invalidated).

**Sprint `3.47` is Done (2026-10-12): a token issued over the in-cluster backchannel must carry the public
issuer.** `charts-api` failed live, after its restore cycle succeeded, with Envoy's `Jwt issuer is not configured`.
The API route accepts the issuer `https://test.resolvefintech.com/auth/realms/prodbox`; the harness's token carries
`http://test.resolvefintech.com:8080/auth/realms/prodbox` (audience and the `prodbox_route` claim are right). Keycloak
is started with `--hostname=<publicHost>` and no scheme, so scheme and port come from the request, and a request
inside the Pod (where the harness issues tokens so the client secrets never leave it) carries no `X-Forwarded-*`
headers. Measured against the pinned `keycloak:26.0.0` in a local container: `--hostname=https://<host>/auth` makes
the issuer `https://<host>/auth/realms/<realm>` for any request, while `--hostname=https://<host>` drops the `/auth`
path. The chart now passes the full public URL; the websocket workload's token exchange and Keycloak's emailed
links share the same request shape and are repaired by the same line; two new cases (red on the chart before),
canonical `prodbox dev check` exits 0 (primary unit **5,573/5,573**). **Live proof: observed 2026-10-12 (`charts-api` passed live after the Keycloak Deployment rolled).** **Deployment
qualification: pending** under Standard P.

**Sprint `5.55` is Done (2026-10-12): the OIDC session validation Job declares what it uses and its script parses.**
`charts-websocket` failed with the bare `OIDC session validation Agent command failed` once Sprint `3.47` had made
`charts-api` pass. The cause was in the namespace's events: the validation Job (one init container and one `curl`
container, memory-backed volumes only) declares CPU and memory and no ephemeral storage, so the namespace
`LimitRange` charged it its default of a 1Gi request and a 2Gi limit, and `vscode-resource-quota` (limits 11,456Mi,
10,432Mi used) refused every Pod the Job tried to create until `kubectl wait` ran out its 180 seconds. Both
containers now declare 32Mi/64Mi. With the Pod admitted the Job died at `sed: unmatched '/'`: the script's
`sed 's/&amp;/\&/g'` was written `\\\&` in Haskell, which the language reads as one backslash plus the empty-string
escape, so the shell saw an escaped delimiter. Run by hand with one backslash fewer, the Job succeeded and printed
the session projection the validation compares. Two cases; canonical `prodbox dev check` exits 0 (primary unit
**5,582/5,582**). **Live proof: observed 2026-10-12 (`charts-websocket` passed its direct OIDC login and upgrade
checks).** **Deployment qualification: pending** under Standard P.

**Sprint `5.54` is Done (2026-10-12): a harness credential whose retained operation expired is replaced, not
resubmitted.** The harness asks the Authority for a credential by resubmitting the intent the Authority already
retains for the operation, so that a response lost after Target material advances recovers the same operation. The
Authority admits an unfinished operation only for byte-identical intent until its thirty-minute deadline and after
it only for a replacement draft that keeps every immutable binding and carries a later deadline. The first
`keycloak-invite` run was refused by the IAM tag read-back (Sprint `2.138`) and left the SMTP operation Authorized;
the retry two hours later resubmitted that intent and the Authority answered `prepared-target/deadline-expired`,
and would have for as long as the operation existed. The resolver now resubmits the retained intent when its
operation completed or its deadline is ahead of the host clock, and otherwise compiles the draft a first request
would send, with the retained action and generation; five new cases, canonical `prodbox dev check` exits 0
(primary unit **5,573/5,573**). **Live proof: observed 2026-10-12 (the Authority accepted the fresh draft and recovered the expired authorized attempt).** **Deployment qualification: pending** under Standard P.

**Sprint `8.13` is Done (2026-10-13): the SMTP identity had a design, a model and a worker, and no caller.** The
first live `keycloak-invite` run failed at Keycloak, whose realm had no SMTP server because
`secret/keycloak/smtp` held nothing: the Keycloak chart's Vault init container logged `No value found` and
continued (the incident plan's `B10`, now observed), and no production code had ever submitted the permit that
creates the retained SES SMTP key family. The permit vocabulary, the worker's SMTP execution (IAM identity,
policy and key, a bounded-memory derived source sealed into retained-home custody, delivery to the sink), the
`TargetSesSmtp` lane and the class-generic coordinator all exist; `mkSesSmtpIamParameters` has no caller,
`firstReconcileIamParameters` refuses the class, the retained SES preparation's `sync-target` stage is a label,
and `Prodbox.Ses.Workflow` has no production importer. The sprint extracts the harness's single credential
submission from the Lifecycle-provider reconcile that `aws-iam` proves live, instantiates it for the retained
SES SMTP family in a stable operation scope, and runs it before the body of the home suites that send an invite.
Sprint `7.47`'s decision `D7` assumed the home arm already delivered; it did not. **Live proof: observed (2026-10-13)**, recorded in the sprint block
(nothing has run); the first run is also the first run of the Provisioner, custody and delivery for SMTP.
Focused group **6/6**; canonical `prodbox dev check` exits 0 (primary unit **5,563/5,563**). **Deployment
qualification: pending.**

**Sprint `1.93` is Done (2026-10-08): the native AWS clients read back the text they write.** The first live
`dns-aws` run failed in its first prerequisite: the Provider wrote the SES verification TXT record and reported
that the read-back did not converge, the observed value being the token wrapped in the literal text `&quot;`.
Route 53 returns a TXT value in XML-escaped quotation marks; the shared XML helper had an escaper for the
requests it emits and no unescaper for the text it extracts, so a value with a quotation mark, an ampersand or an
angle bracket could never read back equal to what was written, and only the emit side of the request body had a
fixture. `xmlUnescape` is the new inverse (five entities and numeric references, one pass, bounded, leaf text
only) and the Route 53 value, name and cursor readers and the AWS error message use it. Focused cases **10/10**
added to the native-client group; canonical `prodbox dev check` exits 0 (primary unit **5,554/5,554**). The native
client runs inside the Provider Worker, so the repair reaches AWS only after the runtime image is rebuilt and the
Provider rolled. **Live proof: observed** — `dns-aws` failed identically before that roll and passed after it
(2026-10-08). **Deployment qualification: pending** on the Provider's DNS lanes under Standard P.

**Sprint `4.106` is Done (2026-10-08): a bootstrap image whose upstream is gone is no longer a pull the
kubelet makes.** The first live `cluster reconcile` of the campaign stopped twice on
`ImagePullBackOff` for `quay.io/minio/mc`. The upstream now issues a token and then refuses the manifest and
tag-list requests (HTTP 401, for `quay.io/minio/minio` and `mc`, and for Docker Hub's `minio/*`), and the
kubelet's garbage collection, which prodbox runs at 70 % high and 60 % low, removed the unused image between the
two Jobs that need it once the reconcile's own image build had taken the disk over 70 %. A rebuilt cluster, whose
containerd is empty, could not have started MinIO at all, which is the first thing each of Sprint `6.5`'s
recover-to-clean cycles does. `Prodbox.Infra.BootstrapImageSeed` now owns the policy (containerd lists the name:
leave it; the host Docker cache holds it: import; neither: pull into the cache, then import; every import read
back; every refusal names the image and both remedies), and `ensureBootstrapImagesSeeded` runs it inside
`ensureMinioRuntime`, before the registry bucket Job, before the gateway MinIO bootstrap Job and in the harness
restore step. Home substrate only. Focused group **10/10**; canonical `prodbox dev check` exits 0 (primary unit **5,544/5,544**); `prodbox test integration cli` **74/74**. **Two things remain the operator's:** the AWS
substrate's nodes pull these images themselves (decision `D8` of Sprint `7.47`, with three images measured
available and not vetted), and a host whose Docker cache lacks the two images has no source. **Live proof: the
kubelet-collection arm is observed** (the fourth live reconcile of the campaign found the `mc` image gone and restored it
from the Docker cache before the Job that needs it); **the rebuilt-cluster arm is pending** — the first recover-to-clean
cycle. **Deployment qualification: pending** on the home reconcile under Standard P.

**Sprint `4.105` is Done (2026-10-05): a Provider session outlives the operation it serves.** The
session was a fixed 900 seconds for an operation allowed thirty minutes, so a destroy that kept
retrying one dependency error past the fifteenth minute failed on an expired credential and the
credential error replaced the cause. `Prodbox.ControlPlane.OperationBudget` now derives the
requested duration from the signed deadline plus a five-minute read-back grace, between the
900-second STS floor and the role's declared 3,600-second maximum. The native STS client carries
the parsed expiry, a session with no usable window starts no work, and each Pulumi child is bounded
by the smaller of the child maximum and the window left. A `dev check` rule refuses a number
assigned to a session duration in the Provider modules. Focused groups pass: budget **12/12**,
duration rule **2/2**, STS **7/7**. The declared maximum is inferred rather than read, and the
ledger registers that gap. **Deployment qualification: pending** on destructive cleanup under
Standard P.

**Sprint `4.104` is Done (2026-10-05): a Pulumi destroy refreshes, continues and cannot outlive its
bound.** The destroy now passes `--refresh --continue-on-error` (both confirmed on the pinned
3.228.0 binary) and never `--clear-pending-creates`, which belongs to `pulumi refresh`. Every Pulumi
child runs under a killable runner that leads its own process group, stops it with SIGTERM and then
SIGKILL, keeps the transcript a stopped child had written, and runs the same stop if its caller is
cancelled; a bound strictly inside the intent lifetime lets the innermost bound fire first. The
runner's six cases pass in the unit suite and in a standalone harness built without `-threaded`, as
the production executable is. Whether a SIGKILLed destroy is resumable is not established until a
live interrupted destroy. **Deployment qualification: pending** on destructive cleanup under
Standard P.

**Sprint `4.103` is Done (2026-10-05): a failed Provider apply names its cause, not only its last
consequence.** The operator saw the first 4,096 characters of a transcript, escaped again by `show`
at three layers, so a final credential-expiry error displaced the dependency error before it.
`Prodbox.ControlPlane.ProviderFailureSummary` names the first AWS error as the cause and the last
differing one as the consequence ahead of a bounded head and tail, classification of stack-command
output reads the whole transcript, the apply callback distinguishes a failed apply from a lost
response, and the execution, Worker-client and Authority-client errors each carry a detail
unchanged. The focused groups pass (summary **12/12**, apply-label case **1/1**). No real Pulumi
transcript is committed, so the first live failure after the image roll is the real test of the
fixture's wording.

**Sprint `4.102` is Done (2026-10-05): a destroy that fails no longer hides the independent
destroys after it.** `reconcileAbsent` attempts every present resource and blocks only one whose
prerequisite failed, was not attempted, or could not be observed. The per-run stacks carry no
success edge; the operational batch keeps its chain (lease role, then user, then the `aws.*`
block). The outcome names what failed and what was not attempted, an exception is a failed destroy,
and an interrupt still propagates. The cases a continue-all fold fails pass. Positional
`reconcileAbsent` remains the callback-era surface the doctrine removes with Sprint `6.5`'s
cutover, and the ledger registers it. **Deployment qualification: pending** on destructive cleanup
under Standard P.

**Sprint `7.45` is Done (2026-10-07): the Provider role's permissions policy is held complete against
the AWS CLI verbs its interpreters run.** `Prodbox.Lifecycle.CredentialProvisioner.ProviderCliActions`
names the IAM actions each verb is authorized by, and `prodbox dev check` fails when a Provider-run
module invokes a verb the table does not name, when the policy lacks a named action, or when a module
chooses its verb at run time without declaring the verbs it may choose. Reading the verbs against the
policy found seven actions no run had reached (the SES DKIM attributes, the receipt-rule describe and
update, the active-rule-set describe, the capture bucket's tag read and write, and the owned-resource
tag listing), and the policy now allows them. The role-policy revision the credential operation scope
derives from the document moves, so the next harness run selects a successor operation. Canonical
`prodbox dev check` exits 0 (primary unit **5,424/5,424**). **Live proof: pending.**

**Sprint `7.44` is Done (2026-10-05): the EKS client-auth identity parse no longer refuses every
well-formed ARN.** The admission split the identity evidence on colons and bound the fourth field,
which the leading `arn` field made the empty region, so the 2026-09-29 drain refused before it
reached a cluster. `Prodbox.Aws.StsIdentity` now owns the marker, the 2,048-character bound, the
renderer and the parser; the admission, the operator identity probe and the Provider's producer
use it, and the probe's second splitter is retired. The focused group passes **26/26**, and a
verbatim copy of the pre-fix parse returns nothing for all seven real shapes.

**Sprint `4.101` is Done (2026-09-23): an existing empty checkpoint cannot mint provider
absence.** `CheckpointEmpty` now becomes `ResidueUnreachable` with the exact stack and cause. The
destroy-only projection remains empty by design, while `resourcesUnobserved`, the per-run
reconcile, and the cascade substrate gate retain the observation and fail closed; no destroy is
silently skipped as success. A genuinely absent checkpoint and the corrupt-checkpoint diagnostic
retain their previous meanings.

This corrects Sprint `4.89` by name without discarding its useful split: readable residue and
capability custody remain separate questions, and an absent or empty checkpoint still means lost
custody. Its earlier empty-to-absence answer was defensible when residue was treated as a projection
of checkpoint contents — there was no Pulumi destroy input — but the 2026-09-07 and 2026-09-16 live
leaks prove that the checkpoint store cannot attest to provider absence. Focused proof **2/2**;
`prodbox test unit` exits 0 with primary unit **5,172/5,172** and every auxiliary stanza green;
canonical `prodbox dev check` exits 0. **Deployment qualification: pending** on destructive cleanup
under Standard P.

**Sprint `4.100` is Done (2026-09-17): the two `cluster delete` exits that explain least now name
the store an operator deletes next.** `retainedStateNarrationFor` was silent on both no-install
arms, so a cascade that reached no phase — the exit whose very next question is whether the retained
root may now be removed — said nothing about it at all. Both arms narrate now, and the silent case
is deleted rather than left unmapped: a narration nothing can select is a case a reader looks for
and never finds. Each arm's sentence is its own, which the previous shape could not manage by
sharing one: a run that uninstalled nothing no longer says "this uninstall", and a cascade that
attempted no destroy no longer says destroys "were attempted earlier in this cascade".

**The confirmed no-install result is a type rather than a fifth table row, and that is the whole
design.** The entry table decides from delete mode and install presence, and neither observes AWS,
so a row that could carry a confirmed result is a row that could mint one from silence — which is
the defect Sprint `4.88` closed once. `ConfirmedNoInstallCascade` has an unexported constructor and
one producer that takes the postflight sweep, admitting exactly the two answers
`decideCascadeUninstallGate` admits; a `checkSealedConstructors` row fails the build if that export
list ever widens. So "never mint success from silence" is a fact the gate holds rather than a
property of a table somebody must keep reading correctly. What the sprint does *not* do is reach it:
`confirmCascadeNoInstall` is representable and uncalled, because the no-install path runs no sweep (**superseded 2026-10-07 by Sprint `6.6`**, which gives that path its sweep and its one caller).
That boundary is the deliverable's own, and `cli_command_surface.md`'s Target region already says
the current revision can reach only the non-zero exit.

**The inventory that arm renders was making two false claims.** It called the retained root
"MinIO-backed per-run Pulumi state" — one writer of a multi-writer capability store that also holds
the Vault durable anchor, the bootstrap unlock bundle, the Lifecycle Authority's records including
Sprint `7.41`'s write-ahead ownership manifests, every registered stack's checkpoint including the
long-lived `aws-ses` one nothing may reap, and the container-registry blobs — and it printed a
hardcoded `.data/` beside the resolved root, so a host whose `manual_pv_host_root` points elsewhere
was shown a path it does not use. It prints the resolved root once and names the classes.

Two gates refused this before it passed, both correctly: the coordinate-hygiene rule caught a
literal AWS region inside a test fixture's ARN, and the wire-fidelity rule caught an inventory
heading that rendered a plain local uninstall and a cascade that had just run every phase against
AWS to the same string. Entry-arm group **6/6**, primary unit **5,171/5,171**, both
`prodbox test integration cli` and `prodbox test integration env` at **70/70**, canonical
`prodbox dev check` exits 0. **Live-proof: pending** — the arm table and its narration are pure, and
a live host exhibiting the silence is evidence rather than a gate.

**Sprint `2.135` is Done and Phase 2 recloses (2026-09-17): the retained-TLS lane can step past one
object it can never write, and exactly one.** Sprint `6.5`'s campaign stopped five consecutive times
on the same node, and the fifth cycle produced the fact rather than another refusal: the Authority's
current retained version is `v2` while the store holds a `v3` object that is a well-formed envelope
whose wrapped DEK does not open under `prodbox-tls-retention-dek`. Both obvious repairs were already
eliminated — rewriting the slot is impossible because a retain draws a fresh DEK and nonce per call
so the bytes are not reproducible, and adopting it is impossible because its DEK is not ours — and
`nextRetentionVersion` returns that version on every future retain, so one unusable object stopped
every retain on that slot forever. The lane now admits one successor past it, from a committed
current reference only.

**The design decision that matters is that the evidence is durable, and the reason is a property of
the validator rather than a preference.** `validateTlsRetentionState` re-runs each outbox's own
staging decision against a state rebuilt from the durable record alone, on both encode and decode,
so any admission input that is not in the record is an input the codec boundary cannot see — and a
version jump authorized by such a token would fail to load the very state that authorized it. The
skipped version and the digest of the bytes that occupied it are therefore retained, and the digest
is not decoration: without it the evidence would be derivable from the candidate, the validator
would be comparing a value against itself, and the skip would be unconditionally admitted.

**The bound is one version and it is enforced in four independent places, because "bounded" is the
whole claim.** The skipped version is pinned to the one the committed reference was about to claim,
so the lane cannot walk forward looking for a free slot; the candidate is pinned to that version's
immediate successor, so there is no jump of two; the transition is reachable from no state but a
committed current reference, so a second skip stacked on a staged successor is a concurrent-pending
refusal; and the successor slot is itself observed before it is claimed, so an occupied successor
refuses by name rather than starting the search the other three forbid. That last refusal is what
gave `TlsWorkflowRetentionVersionOccupied` a producer — Sprint `6.5` declared, classified and
rendered it, then chose adoption over refusal and left it constructible nowhere.

**The new durable state is the only recovery outbox that retains its predecessor, and that is not
symmetry with the legacy lane but a difference from it.** Every pre-outbox recovery state answers
`Nothing` for a current reference because it is entered from an empty aggregate, where none exists.
This one is entered from a committed reference whose own object is intact; only the successor slot
is unwritable. So restore keeps applying that reference for the whole staging window — which matters
because the retain that stages the skip runs on the vscode chart delete and the matching restore
runs on the deploy — and promotion is still judged against it for staleness, validity regression and
key change. The constructor is appended, so both byte-pinned pre-outbox encodings and every
intermediate wire tag are unchanged, which the existing codec cases prove by continuing to pass
untouched.

**One success is now announced, because no failure line would ever carry it.** The Authority's
protected-log emitter fires only on `Left`, so a retain that succeeded while permanently abandoning
an immutable object would leave the skip recorded in a durable Authority field and nowhere a reader
looks. A promoted successor writes
`tls-retention/workflow notice=retained-past-unopenable-version/v<n>`, distinct from the refusal
line in both key and token. The deployed `TlsRetentionWorkflowAuthorityFailure` vocabulary is
deliberately not widened: the successor succeeds and answers the existing retained response, and
where no successor is admissible the existing `retention-version-unopenable/v<n>` remains the
refusal.

**An adversarial review after the change was green found three defects the gates and the tests had
both agreed with, and all three are repaired.** `validateUnopenableSuccessorStaging` compared the
evidence, candidate and envelope but not the approval or the predecessor, so an Authority returning
a pending with an approval the host never sent would have been accepted — and promotion uses the
pending's own approval; it now compares the complete record, as its three siblings do. The Target
Secret Agent's per-attempt request bound was left unchanged on the argument that the Authority-lane
branches are mutually exclusive with the pre-outbox ones — true at one retain, false across one
attempt, because a first retain that enters empty and promotes leaves the aggregate current for the
retain-on-ready that follows it; the two summands are added, taking the maximum to 38, the replay
capacity to 76 and the encoded ceiling to 154 MiB, which in turn does not fit the Vault listener's
former 192 MiB request ceiling once Base64-expanded, so that moves to 224 MiB and its comment stops
describing a 112 MiB projection it has not had for some time. And two governed sentences were false
rather than incomplete: "every recovery state refuses restore and issuance", which this sprint's
state contradicts by design, and "`validateTlsRetentionState` re-runs each outbox's own staging
decision", which holds for two of the five pending constructors. The same pass also softened an
evidence Haddock that claimed more than a pure fold can know, and closed a false success where a
`404` from the selected Agent reported nothing-to-retain while leaving a durable outbox bound to a
source that had vanished.

**Three findings are registered rather than closed, and one of them is about this sprint's own
premise.** The TLS Retention Adapter's replay capacity is the undifferentiated generic 4 and was
never derived for that role; counting the Adapter requests one retain issues, the deepest pre-outbox
recovery path already reaches five, so the bound is exceeded on paper by a path that predates this
sprint. Nothing is raised, because exhausting it is a live refusal no host has reported and moving a
Standard-P capacity on a paper argument is the unmeasured change this plan exists to prevent; the
ledger carries it `Unowned` so the measurement is owed. And the sprint block's claim that the two
lanes are "kept disjoint by the frozen counterexample
`TLS-LEGACY-RECOVERY-V3-IMMUTABLE-COLLISION-2026-09-08`" overstates that identifier: it has no
fixture family, no loader and no derived rows, and its entire executable content is two string
equalities over the two object-name constructors. What it freezes is the key-space partition, not
any staging behaviour. The disjointness this sprint relies on is enforced by the two staging
decisions' own state gates — pre-outbox recovery from `TlsRetentionEmpty` only, the successor from
`TlsRetentionCurrent` only — and is asserted directly rather than inherited. The third is Sprint
`6.5`'s rather than this sprint's: the resumed-collision rebase onto an occupied Authority-lane
version can never commit, because its success path routes through the ordinary staging transition
and the desired pending necessarily differs from the durable one by the very envelope mismatch that
caused the collision. It does real Target work for an outcome fixed in advance, and superseding a
pending with an occupant-derived one needs an Authority-side transition that does not exist. It is
registered here because this sprint's successor outbox reaches the same arm.

That last one was the review's strongest finding and the only one to survive three independent
refutation attempts from two lenses, and the part worth keeping is what the dead path was doing on
the way to failing. It ran a live selected retain and a live restore into the public-edge Secret
before the Authority refused it, and the refusal arrived as `authority-state-unavailable` — an
occupied immutable slot reported as an unavailable Authority, which is the misattribution four live
cycles of this campaign were spent removing. The same arm emitted its "resumed slot occupied"
refusal only on the branch where the re-read said the slot was *missing*. Both are repaired: the arm
re-observes and refuses by name with no Target work, and each constructor now sits on the branch its
own documentation describes.

Stable counterexample `TLS-AUTHORITY-UNOPENABLE-VERSION-PERMANENT-RETAIN-STOP-2026-09-15` is
registered with a repository-owned two-sided reproducer whose causal profile is one constructed
durable state and no infrastructure at all. Authority fold **34/34**, TLS-retention endpoint
**35/35**, control-plane route **9/9**, primary unit **5,169/5,169**, both
`prodbox test integration cli` and `prodbox test integration env` at **70/70**, canonical
`prodbox dev check` exits 0. **Live-proof: pending** — no live host has run the successor transition, and no fake can
establish that a real retained-home Transit key refuses the exact object a live store holds.

**Sprint `7.42` is Done and Phase 7 recloses (2026-09-15): the one mechanism that can recover a live
resource named by nothing now has a way in.** The adoption observer, its planner, the permit
admission and the receipt repository were written, tested, and called from nothing — not because
anyone forgot a call, but because the authorization half had no surface. It is now two verbs.
`prodbox aws stack <eks|test|aws-subzone> adopt-legacy plan` observes the closed registry-derived
family through the read-only Provider capability and prints the exact candidate document with the
digest taken over those bytes; `... adopt-legacy apply --plan-digest <digest> --yes` observes and
renders **again** and confirms the operator's digest against the plan *that* pass produced, then
receipt-commits and independently reads back. The second observation is the deliverable's real
content: carrying the first pass's document forward would authorize a candidate set nobody
re-checked against the world, and a plan re-rendered after the provider facts changed is a different
plan the operator never saw. Retained `aws-ses` has no adoption verb, because a per-run cleanup
ownership record over the one stack nothing may reap is the same category error the run-scoped tag
keeps it out of.

**The sprint's second deliverable turned out to be a claim that was false rather than merely
unstated.** It asked that the result be "cleanup-only provenance with no type-level path into a
future create" — and `proveWriteAheadOwnership` accepted any complete manifest. An adoption commits
a `CompleteOwnershipManifest` and reads it back through the same projection a create does, so a
record of resources somebody else made would have minted the create-side proof that type's own GADT
index says it may not; the index could not see it because the purpose was a field the decision view
did not carry. The view carries it now and the minter refuses the adoption arm, and the receipt is
an opaque `AdoptedCleanupOwnership` with no projection back to that evidence at all. The synthetic
mutation was written, compiled, rejected, and reverted rather than asserted.

**One property of the mechanism is worth stating because its first draft got it wrong.** The
composition root gave all four family members a single Authority dispatch key. The submission key is
the Authority's idempotency identity, so the second, third and fourth observations would have
replayed the first's evidence — four well-formed answers about one resource, which is an ambiguity
the planner's five refusals cannot detect. `legacyAdoptionDispatchKeyFor` now derives one key per
member from the intent's own coordinate, stable across re-runs so a repeated plan pass replays the
retained observation rather than allocating a new identity for one question.

**A second finding is about a rule that was describing a projection that did not exist.**
`ValidatedCoordinates` parsed `aws_substrate.subzone_name` and discarded it while
`tier0CoordinateReadRegistry` listed the field as having a projection, so the subzone adoption had
nothing validated to read and the honest alternative was a raw read of the kind an open ledger row
already names. The projection is added.

**`prodbox dev check` refused the change twice before it passed, both times correctly.** Deleting
the six `unconsumedTypedGuardRegistry` rows the closed ledger row owned left four cleanup-authority
projections with no production consumer. One gained a real one — the operator output prints the run
scope the receipt is keyed under, which is how a reader finds the object a later cleanup will read.
The three `AdminLegacyAdoptionPermit` projections had none and are deleted: a permit is a token
rather than a record, and accessors that read a proof's contents back out are how a caller starts
re-deciding what the admission already decided. The consequence is stated rather than hidden — the
nonce is now unobservable outside its module, which is correct only while nothing records permits
durably.

**A third defect was in the gate that was asked to hold the new claims.** Registering the four
adoption unconstructibility claims in `checkSealedConstructors` made it refuse
`LegacyAdoptionPlan` — whose export list does not expose its constructors. `moduleExportListIn`
returned the whole module header joined with spaces, and
`Prodbox.Lifecycle.Teardown.LegacyAdoptionPlan` ends with the exact type name, so the export list's
own opening parenthesis read as that type exporting its constructors; the boundary check could not
object, because the character before the name is a dot. It returns only the parenthesised list now.
Adoption lane **9/9**, planner **13/13**, observer **3/3**, receipt repository **5/5**,
write-ahead ownership **26/26**, primary unit **5,159/5,159**, canonical `prodbox dev check`
exits 0.

**What the sprint does not claim is registered rather than implied.** Nothing consumes the identity
allowlist the receipt records: the lane ends before any mutation, and turning that allowlist into a
destroy is Sprint `6.5`'s single-writer cutover. And no live adoption has run — a fake provider
cannot establish that a real Provider answer decodes into the closed family, or that the committed
receipt reads back byte-identically from the retained Authority. Both are `Live-proof: pending` and
non-blocking under Standard O.

**Sprint `6.5`'s three non-activation deliverables landed 2026-09-14, and they are the ones that
were never gated on the campaign.** The postflight tag sweep passed no region and read one response
body, so it saw one region, one page, and — because the Tagging API returns IAM only from the
global-service region — no IAM role at all, which is why the 2026-09-07 residue had to be cleared by
hand from outside the product. It now issues each filter in the run's region and in the
global-service region through the same bounded cursor-following listing the compiled audit uses. It
runs *before* the local uninstall and gates it: an unconfirmed or non-empty sweep leaves the local
control plane running, because it is the only surface permitted to mutate AWS and destroying it is
what turned detection into detection without remediation. And whether the sweep is owed now comes
from the declared substrate (since widened by Sprint `6.6` to any authored AWS coordinate) rather than from three per-run checkpoints reading absent — a checkpoint
is Pulumi state, and its absence is exactly the condition under which a resource is most likely to be
stranded.

A defect no bullet named surfaced while repairing it: the superseded parser dropped a returned
resource whose tag list it could not read, which is residue becoming absence in the same direction
as the page and region blindness. A tagless row is now kept, attributed to the filter that returned
it, and reaches the escaped list.

**A second finding came from auditing the sprint's validation items against the tree, and it is
about a claim rather than a behaviour.** Sprint `6.5`'s item 3 says a dual-writer cutover state and
a post-activation legacy rollback cannot be constructed; Sprint `7.41`'s item 2 says an execute that
skips the read-back does not compile. Both are true, and both are true only while the constructors
stay inside their modules — widening `CutoverState` to `CutoverState (..)` would void them without
changing a line of logic, and no test could notice, because the test that would notice is the one
that cannot be written. `checkSealedConstructors` now holds the nine types whose unconstructibility
claim is load-bearing — including the three cascade-evidence values this sprint's own validation
calls private, whose seal lives in a public facade rather than in the module that declares them, and
the recovery-plane final evidence whose `Lost` constructor retains the very readiness proof its sole
eliminator withholds. It refuses an export list naming any of their constructors and refuses a
registry row whose declaring module no longer declares the type or whose facade no longer exports
it, and it was proven to refuse against the freshly built binary in all three shapes, not only to
pass. A second rule followed from the same reading, for claims about a *name* rather
than a constructor: `CascadeCandidate`'s facade says the drive stays package-private *"so holding
one of these booleans authorizes nothing and cannot start a cascade"* — this sprint's validation
item 4 stated in a Haddock — and `checkFacadeWithholdings` now refuses a facade that re-exports it.
What the gates do not reach is registered rather than implied: a facade seal bounds the public
boundary, while the declaring `…Internal` module still hands its constructors to its 18 importers,
so *private* in that validation item is true of the boundary it names and weaker than it reads. Cascade group **139/139**, tag sweep **22/22**,
uninstall gate **8/8**, sealed and withheld exports **27/27**, primary unit **5,136/5,136**, canonical
`prodbox dev check` exits 0.

**Two measurements from the 2026-09-15 audit pass, neither of which lands code.** The four
counterexamples this campaign closed code-locally were re-verified against a tree that has since
taken Sprints `4.95`–`4.99`, `5.47`–`5.48` and `7.41`; all four hold. And the ~19 minutes every live
cycle spends rebuilding is now a measured decision rather than an accepted cost: the Dockerfile
copies `src/` before its single `cabal build`, so a one-line change rebuilds every dependency, and
the obvious layer split would add the measured **5.8 GB** dependency store to the shipped image
because layers are additive and BuildKit cache mounts are forbidden by doctrine. The repair that
gets both is a builder stage, which is a doctrine change on a Standard-P component-image surface and
is recorded rather than taken.

**Sprint `6.5`'s code-local validation matrix was re-run on 2026-09-15, which is the part of that
row a session can actually discharge while the campaign is pending.** Every scope exits 0:
`prodbox dev check`; `prodbox test unit` over **5,160** primary cases plus authority admission
**27/27**, control-plane authentication **35/35**, authenticated transport **39/39**, Haskell style
**17/17** and Pulumi **4/4**; and both `prodbox test integration cli` and `prodbox test integration
env`, each running the `prodbox-integration` stanza at **70/70**. Sole-writer status was re-verified
against the tree rather than restated: the four cutover functions and `LegacyScanPostActivation`
still occur only in `Prodbox.Test.CleanRoomHandoff`, and `prodbox cluster delete --cascade` still
routes to `runNativeDeleteCascade`. The item is standing rather than one-shot — it is owed again on
every revision that reaches this row.

**What is left of Sprint `6.5` is the activation, and the campaign that gates it is running again
as of 2026-09-15.** Standard P forbids activation and legacy deletion until a current-revision home
qualification row is `proven`, which needs two consecutive live destructive candidate cycles. The
blocker recorded here through 2026-09-14 — no `test-secrets.dhall`, which carries the durable
elevated AWS credential that by [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md#security) enters `prodbox` only through the
interactive `SecretRef.Prompt` — **is lifted**: the operator restored the file, and the harness
regenerates the Tier-0 `prodbox.dhall` from it through
`regenerateConfigFromTestSecrets`, so no interactive `config setup` was needed and the first cycle
installed RKE2 onto a genuine clean-room host and brought the full local control plane up.

**Three cycles have run and none has completed one, which is the campaign working rather than
failing.** Each refused before candidate execution, each refusal was attributable, and each was
repaired code-locally with `prodbox dev check` at 0 before the next launched.

The first refusal was in **Sprint `7.41`'s own write-ahead mechanism, on its first live exercise**:
a create commits its ownership manifest under `ReconcileDesiredPresent` — its own side of the
lifecycle — and then read the manifest back through the *cleanup-side* read-back while still passing
that create-side scope. `mkOwnershipManifestTarget` mints its binding under `ReconcileDesiredAbsent`
because a target is cleanup authority's vehicle, so the two are mutually exclusive by construction
and every live create refused. Nothing leaked: the refusal is before the effect, and a read-only
all-region sweep found no EKS cluster and no non-default VPC. The read-back now asks on the cleanup
side, which is also the more honest statement of what it is for — the create is asking the question
a later teardown will ask, not taking a second look at what it just wrote. **Both unit suites over
this lane hand-built the cleanup-side scope in a fixture**, so what they held was a relationship an
author had already got right rather than the one production passes; four cases now assert the
production re-scoper.

The second refusal came on the **second consecutive cycle, which is precisely what the two-cycle
requirement exists to reach**. The public-edge TLS retain that runs before the vscode chart delete
writes its Authority-lane object with a put-if-absent and never observes that lane first — the
observation above it reads the *legacy* lane, to answer the different question of whether there is a
pre-Authority envelope to adopt. When the store's occupancy has drifted ahead of the Authority's
current version, which is what an interrupted retain leaves, the claim collides and surfaces as
`put/conflict/confirmation/bytes-mismatch`: a refusal naming neither the version nor either digest.
An ordinary retain now observes before it claims and refuses by name. The occupant is deliberately
not adopted, because adoption on that lane would promote an envelope nothing staged; and the public
failure vocabulary is deliberately not widened, because that is a deployed-protocol change.

**The third cycle then proved that refusal was aimed at the wrong arm, which is the more useful
result.** It ran the repaired runtime — the Authority pod's `imageID` is the manifest that cycle
pushed — and still reported the opaque store conflict, so the new observation never ran, so the
retain is not reaching the claim path at all. It is resuming a **pending staged by an earlier run**,
and a resumed pending has no version to claim and no observation ahead of its store. Only the
legacy-recovery state can rebase onto an occupant; every other state returned the adapter's own
error, which is why three consecutive live cycles reported an unavailable adapter for a slot
somebody else held. That catch-all now names the version, with the recovery behaviour unchanged.

**The fourth cycle produced the number, and it names the blocker.** `retention-version-occupied/v3`:
the Authority's current retained version is `v2` while the store already holds `v3` under an
envelope that is not the one the retain builds. That is the skew an interrupted retain leaves — an
object written and a promotion lost — and the ordinary state cannot pass it, because each attempt
wraps a fresh DEK so the bytes are not reproducible and `v3` is immutable. The one mechanism that
could resolve it, rebasing onto the occupant, is gated to the legacy-recovery state. **Until that
skew is resolved this host completes no cycle**, because the retain runs on the vscode chart delete,
the third node of the restore graph. That is the next owed piece of work on Sprint `6.5` and it is
now a stated problem rather than an unattributed refusal.

**Cycle six cleared the blocker and reached further than this campaign ever has.** From the restored
clean-room baseline the restore graph completed with no failed node, and the `aws-eks-subzone` create
returned a Provider receipt — the **first live execution of a registered stack create through the
repaired write-ahead read-back**, so the defect that refused every create is closed live rather than
only code-locally. The `aws-eks` create then failed at the effect with a Provider Worker 503 after
its generation was committed, which is the one arm under which a resource can exist, and it named
the durable manifest that says what it was authorized to make.

**Resources did exist, and the teardown proved the leak class is detected but not remediated.** An
ACTIVE EKS cluster, two `t3.large` nodes, a VPC, an internet gateway and IAM. `cluster delete
--cascade` and `aws stack eks destroy --yes` both answered *absent* from an empty checkpoint — the
false-absence this plan names — while the postflight sweep returned **43 tag-matches** on Sprint
`7.41`'s own provider-side run tags and **gated the uninstall**, leaving the control plane running
because destroying it would leave nothing able to act on the answer. Detection, region and page
coverage, and the ordering repair are live-proven; remediation is the gap, and closing it is exactly
what Sprint `6.5`'s activation owns. The residue was cleared by hand under explicit operator
authorization and the account verified empty in all three regions.

No qualification artifact and no activation witness exists, the legacy public writer remains sole,
and Sprint `6.5` stays open.

**Sprint `7.41`'s core is landed (2026-09-14): a create now says what it is about to make, and the
reader stops laundering its own evidence.** The manifest is committed and read back through a
second, independent call between the generation commit and the execute; the execute step takes a
`WriteAheadOwnershipProof` whose constructor is unexported and whose only minter accepts complete
evidence, so an execute that skips the read-back does not compile; and the append gives the manifest
the identity the provider returned.

**Closing it required absorbing a row this plan had recorded `Unowned` one day earlier.**
`confirmOwnershipManifestDecisionReadBack` degraded *every* arm to observation-only — including a
`Present` arm that successfully decoded a manifest carrying its entries — and the decision ladder
maps that to a refusal. Committing the manifest without changing that arm would have converted a
quiet teardown into a different refusal and bought no destroy path, which the sprint block says
outright. The ledger said that change needed its own sprint; it did not, because Sprint `7.41`
already declares the invalidation it makes. The two minters it consumes were registered unconsumed
guards, and Sprint `5.47`'s gate — landed hours earlier — refused the build until their rows were
deleted in the same change.

**Three things the sprint block did not anticipate, all corrected in the mechanism.** The manifest
cannot be keyed under the caller's creation scope, which carries no AWS coordinates by design and
which the manifest identity refuses; it is keyed under the scope the committed generation proved,
which is the derivation the Authority already uses for the creation binding. The append cannot
rewrite the write-ahead slot, which is immutable by construction; it writes a second object under
the same identity in a completion namespace, and the cleanup read-back prefers the completion and
falls back — so an interrupted create is addressable rather than invisible, and its identity-less
manifest is refused by naming the missing entry rather than by destroying nothing. And that second
object needed two additional wire actions, added as tags with the unknown-tag decode failure intact.

**The two remaining deliverables landed the same day, and the sprint is `Done`.** The provider-side
run pair — `prodbox.io/run-scope` and `prodbox.io/submission` — is stamped by the provider as
`defaultTags` on the default AWS provider of the three per-run programs, so a resource added to a
program carries it without anyone remembering to author it. The measured obstacle closed the way the
sprint said it would: the marker rides inside the intent, minted before the intent is built by a
lane that now takes a builder rather than a value, so one marker reaches both the admit and the
execute and the replay digest stays stable. `aws-ses` is deliberately excluded — a per-run marker on
the retained long-lived stack would tell a per-run sweep that the one stack nothing may reap belongs
to the run currently reaping.

**One consequence is stated rather than hidden.** The pair is projected onto the Pulumi preview as
well as the apply, because a preview run against different configuration than the apply reports an
agreement the apply does not keep — the exact defect
`PROVIDER-WORKER-PULUMI-STACK-CONFIG-ABSENT-2026-09-05` froze. Since the pair is per-submission, a
reconcile of a stack that is already present now previews a tag change and applies it: the marker
the provider holds names the run that last proved it, which is the run whose write-ahead record a
cascade will find.

**The counterexample family `CREATE-INTERRUPTED-2026-09-08` is the fourth on disk, and it separates
the two lanes rather than describing one.** Its rows are derived from each implementation's lane
rather than authored, so editing one fails the load; the superseded lane answers `orphan-unnameable`
at all five interruption kinds at or after its effect and the replacement lane answers
`coordinates-named` at thirty-five points and `orphan-unnameable` at none; and both lanes run the
effect, because an implementation that never mutates never orphans either and is not a fix. The
committed mutation asserts the counterexample's own failure against the implementation that closes
it and must fail to load. The profile pair holds the topology-normalized budget constant, enforced
at load rather than asserted in a test, so the counterexample cannot be closed by spending more.

Create-interrupted oracle **23/23**, write-ahead ownership **14/14**, field-of-view **26/26**,
primary unit **5,094/5,094**, canonical `prodbox dev check` exits 0.

**Sprint `5.48` is Done and Phase 5 recloses (2026-09-14): the repository models the one invariant
a type cannot hold, and registers the ordering under which it fails.** Two models existed and both
were about the gateway. The third is about a create: admit, commit the generation record, commit and
independently read back a write-ahead ownership manifest, dispatch, land, append, settle — and the
two ways a host stops knowing what it did, a transport deadline that cancels the reply and a crash.
The checked property is safety and it asserts naming, never absence: every coordinate that exists in
the provider is named by some durable manifest. "Absent in AWS" is a claim about the world that does
not belong inside a model property any more than inside a type.

**The frozen superseded ordering is registered beside the repaired one and must fail.**
`Prodbox.Tla.TlaModel` now carries a declared disposition, and the 2026-09-08 configuration — a
generation record naming the cycle and nothing naming the resources — is registered as
`ExpectsCounterexample`, so `prodbox dev tla-check` refuses if it *passes*. TLC finds the trace in
five states: admit, commit the generation, dispatch, land, violated. No crash is needed. The
invariant breaks the instant the effect lands ahead of any record of it, which is the
commit-before-effect ordering stated as a trace rather than as a sentence.

**Nothing held the model directory and the model registry against each other.**
`checkTlaModelRegistration` now refuses a `.tla` or `.cfg` file no entry names, an entry no file
backs, and a registry in which no configuration expects a counterexample. A model nobody registers
is a proof surface that does not run — the shape Sprint `5.45` closed for test stanzas and `5.47`
for the suites the gate compiled.

Two corrections the sprint did not anticipate, both in the mechanism rather than in the account of
it. The model's first draft held one manifest slot rather than one per cycle, and TLC found in
eleven steps that a second create erased the first's record; the fix is in the model because it is
also true of the runtime, where a manifest is committed at the submission key. And a configuration
expected to produce a counterexample leaves a trace-expression module and a root-owned `states`
directory in a governed directory on every run, which this host cannot delete — TLC now runs with
`-cleanup` and `-noGenerateSpecTE`. Neither surfaced before, because no registered configuration had
ever failed. The model proves the protocol and never the boundary implementation: it does not prove
that the write-ahead commit is called before the execute step, which is a source fact Sprint `7.41`
owns and Sprint `5.47`'s guard gate currently records as *not* true. Model check **1,750 distinct
states, depth 18, six invariants**, the superseded ordering refused in **5** states, all four
registered configurations satisfied, registration cases **6/6**, primary unit **5,052/5,052**,
canonical `prodbox dev check` exits 0.

**Sprint `5.47` is Done (2026-09-14): the check now reads a `case` arm, and runs what it compiles.**
Two gates landed and a suite route with them. `checkTypedGuardConsumption` refuses a binding whose
declared type names one of the repository's cleanup-authority vocabularies when no module under
`src/` reads it — a value-level guard with no production consumer is not a guard, which the purity
standard states and nothing enforced. The subject is deliberately narrower than the sprint's own
sentence: "a function whose name looks like a guard" selects 208 bindings here, three in five of
them ordinary accessors, and a rule whose registry is larger than its finding set constrains
nothing. Typed by authority instead, the region is 114 declarations of which **41** have no
production consumer, and all 41 are registered against the deletion-ledger row that owns their
consumption.

**Two of the four locations the ledger row named had been found by reading, and the gate found the
other two.** `resourceDestroyCapability` is written into every managed-resource descriptor and read
by nothing, which no call-site rule sees, because a field written into a record literal is not a
read of it. `dischargeByObservedAbsence` has a call site, and it is inside
`fixedCheckpointAbsenceDischargeRegression` — a self-test proves a guard can refuse and is not a
decision that consults it. That second distinction is the one the 2026-09-08 leak turned on.

**The wire-fidelity rule refuses nothing on the tree as it stands, and that is the honest result.**
It reports 24 collapses across 15 functions and every one is registered with its reason, so its
value is entirely prospective: a new collapse fails the build, and the stale-exemption direction
stops the registry drifting into a description of the tree. The 15 were adjudicated against their
consumers one at a time, not waved through — six are the Bootstrap Broker's three-valued boundary
classifiers, whose returned string is the key `boundaryReply` matches to pick an HTTP status and is
emitted verbatim as the body, with the exact cause surviving on the protected baseline diagnostic;
`providerIntentResourceKey` shares one key between an observe and its reap because the key names the
registered family the Authority grants. **One of the 15 is a real defect deferred rather than a
contract**, and it now carries a ledger row: twenty of the Target Secret Worker's twenty-eight
runtime failures reach the coordinator as one token, and widening that vocabulary is a
deployed-protocol change this sprint declares it does not make.

**The rule's own first draft produced three false findings, and the fix went into the rule.**
`renderingArmsIn` joins the arms of every `case` in a body, including `where`-bound ones over
different types, so comparing literals across the whole body read a composite renderer's
`size=empty` and `shape=empty` as one collapsed value. It now compares within each type, which is
what its own sentence said; and a module's own declarations win over the shared index, because a
type two modules declare is dropped from that index and the rule was blind to a renderer written
beside its own type.

**Running the suite the gate compiles surfaced a case that could not run.** `prodbox dev check`
executes `prodbox-unit` and the three auxiliary `-unit` stanzas after the binary sync — **126
seconds** against a gate that already exceeds ten minutes — and `prodbox test all` subtracts them
and says so rather than doubling a five-thousand-case suite. One planner case invoked a real
`kubectl get endpoints kubernetes`: the chart plan builder makes six observations that leave the
process and only the runtime image had a seam. `ChartPlanObservers` names both now. A unit assertion
that cannot execute on the host the gate runs on is not a proof surface, which is the condition the
deliverable exists to remove.

One deliverable was already closed when this sprint reached it and is struck rather than restated:
the ban on absence minted from a substring match over subprocess output landed as Sprint `4.98`'s
`checkAbsenceMinterProvenance` on 2026-09-13, one day after this block was written. Gate cases
**42/42**, each exercised against a synthetic violation and the real tree, primary unit
**5,046/5,046**, auxiliaries **27/27**, **35/35**, **39/39**, canonical `prodbox dev check`
exits 0.

**Sprint `4.99` is Done (2026-09-14): six wire formats became one, and the gate landed after.** The
provider evidence wire typed its payload as bare `Text`, so nothing joined an encoder to the rule it
had to satisfy, and six producers emitted a character `validateProviderIntentEvidence` refuses —
three unconditionally, including the wired desired-absence observation and the cascade's terminal
audit. All six now render through one canonical encoder against a bound the executor supplies;
`ProviderReadOnly` returns a sealed type rather than a bare `Text`, so an encoder cannot return an
unchecked value at all. Five encoders and every private bound they invented are deleted rather than
re-tuned, and `parseLbcFamilyRows` — a second parser that selected which ARNs the reaper *deleted* —
is retired in favour of the rows the encoder was handed.

**Three defects surfaced during the conversion that the sprint had not named.** The terminal audit
emitted its rows in the provider's return order, so two identical listings paginated differently
rendered to different bytes, which the Authority's byte-equality replay comparison reads as a
mismatch — and which no test could have caught while that evidence was refused before ever reaching
the Authority. The audit declared no bound of any kind on a listing that follows pagination to a
hundred pages. And the native family's 128 KiB byte bound and 4,096-identity bound were mutually
unreachable as well as both wrong, which nothing noticed because the newline refused first.

**Two things are stated rather than closed, and both are non-blocking.** The terminal audit's new
listing cardinality is arithmetic derived from what the wire carries, not a measurement of a real
escaping account. And no live cascade has yet carried one of these observations to settlement: the
repair is self-consistent and asserted from both sides, but a unit table cannot establish that a
real provider answer reaches the Authority and settles, or that a re-dispatched operation returns
byte-identical evidence.

**A four-day EKS leak reopened Phases `4`, `5` and `7` (2026-09-12).** A cluster created on
2026-09-08 billed until an operator deleted it by hand, and the cascade that should have removed it
refused with its drain and sweep phases unresolved. The cause is not the cascade. A create was
cancelled by its own transport deadline after its AWS effects had landed; the checkpoint describing
them was never committed, because the commit runs only on the return route and the scratch holding
it lives in RAM; and every later teardown read the missing checkpoint as positive absence. The
reopen widened on 2026-09-13: the observation the corrected decision path depends on cannot settle
either, because its evidence encoder emits characters the Provider Worker's own validator refuses.
The generation record was committed one second before the capability ran, so the cycle was
addressable —
but a generation names a cycle, not resources, and the write-ahead ownership manifest that would
have named them has no production writer.

**The wider finding is that this class has recurred four times and the type system cannot close
it.** Thirty-four sprints have applied a type-level device to cleanup, absence and residue. Each
makes a value unconstructible and each claim is true; none makes an outcome in a cloud account
unconstructible, and the doctrine already says none may. Three consequences are now scheduled rather
than restated: absence is minted from a substring match on a subprocess's error output and laundered
into the strongest absence type in the tree; the typed decision ladder is reachable only from the
qualification harness while the shipping cascade runs on exit codes; and the guards that would have
caught all of it are written, tested, and called from nothing. Sprint `0.34` places the statement
where a new sprint meets it, and Sprints `4.95` through `7.42` do the work.

**The ephemeral Kubernetes client authenticated to an EKS API server for the first time
(2026-09-12).** Live cascade-qualification cycle `recovery-ephemeral-credential-file` reached and
passed the drain commit's Kubernetes UID observation. The proof is structural rather than
inferred: the refusal it now stops at is reachable only from the present-UID arm of
`acquireVerifiedEksDrainSelection`, and the refusal every prior cycle produced,
`EksDrainCommitSelectionKubernetesUidUnobservable`, appears zero times in the transcript. That is
the live half of Sprints `7.39` and `7.40`.

The cycle still exits 1, on a defect that only became reachable because they landed. The drain
commit asks for a lease of exactly `maximumEksDrainLifetimeSeconds`, 900 seconds, while
`mkEksDrainSession` also requires the deadline not to outlive the Provider-issued bearer that backs
it. ~~That bearer is signed before the deadline is computed, so a lease equal to the ceiling can
never satisfy both.~~ Stable counterexample
`CASCADE-QUALIFICATION-EKS-DRAIN-LEASE-EXCEEDS-BEARER-EXPIRY-2026-09-12` owns it.

**Sprint `4.95` is Done and the account above is corrected in place (2026-09-12, Standard C).** The
struck sentence runs the inference backwards and is retired rather than deleted, because it is the
reading a reader is most likely to repeat: the mint happens *later* than the clock read the deadline
is computed from, and a later mint yields a later expiry, which relaxes the bearer bound. The
observed refusal proves ordering contributed nothing — `deadline - now` is exactly the lease, so
both clock reads returned the same second. What is true needs no ordering: both comparisons are
strict, so a deadline equal to the ceiling passes the ceiling and only the bearer bound can have
failed; and it must fail for any lease at the ceiling, because the Provider's own mint refuses a
bearer whose expiry exceeds the same 900-second bound measured from a clock read no earlier than
this one.

The repair is two things, and the second is the one that unblocks the campaign. The three deadline
bounds now have three refusals instead of two, and the bearer arm carries the expiry it compared
against, which is the measurement instrument the next live cycle needs. And the lease stops being
the ceiling: it is derived from the bounded work a drain commit issues before its first mutation —
six ephemeral calls at the ephemeral client's own per-invocation bound, plus one call's slack — with
`mkEksDrainLeaseSeconds` refusing anything shorter, so the derivation is enforced rather than merely
used. Nothing clamps; a lease above what the bearer can back still refuses, and now says so. The
credential's own lifetime remains unmeasured, which is exactly what the widened refusal exists to
capture.

**Sprint `7.40` is Done and Phase 7 recloses (2026-09-11).** The ephemeral Kubernetes client's
machinery has one statement, held there by a gate rather than by a sentence.
`withEksKubeconfig` is routed onto the owning module and keeps its four callers; its duplicate
kubeconfig renderer, its named pipe, its unsupervised writer and five orphaned imports are gone. The
copies had drifted exactly as the argument predicted — one created its pipe owner-read-write and the
other owner-all, and only one wrote its kubeconfig with `O_EXCL`, `O_NOFOLLOW`, `CLOEXEC`, an
explicit mode and an fsync — so a pre-placed path could capture one and not the other.

Two things about that sprint are worth carrying forward. The rule reads its two markers in different
places, and the first draft was wrong about it: read as a bare token, `tokenFile` fired on an
ordinary binder for a projected service-account JWT path, which is refusing a word rather than a
second statement of a security property. The writer is a Haskell name and is read with string
literals stripped; the rendered key is read only inside literals, which is the only place a second
statement could put it. And the false positive was invisible to `prodbox dev check`, which exited 0
on a stale `./.build/prodbox` — the gate runs in-process, so a check binary that predates the gate
validates nothing. Gate cases **5/5**, exercised against the real tree as well as synthetically,
primary unit **4,966/4,966**, canonical `prodbox dev check` exits 0.

**Sprint `7.39` is Done (2026-09-11).** The ephemeral Kubernetes client has a credential mechanism
that works, and the measurement is what chose it. The design question the sprint opened with was
whether a FIFO earns its complexity; the deciding question turned out to be how many times the
reader reads, which no reasoning about the kubeconfig contract would have answered. Under `strace`,
`kubectl` v1.35.8 opens its token file **exactly twice per invocation and independently of request
count** — twice for `version`, which makes none, twice for `--raw`, which makes one, twice for a
discovery-bearing `get`, which makes six. A rendezvous must therefore serve the credential at least
twice, to a reader whose arrival it cannot observe, which retires the rendezvous as a class rather
than one broken implementation of it.

The credential is now a file written with `O_EXCL`, `O_NOFOLLOW`, `CLOEXEC` and mode `0600` beside
the kubeconfig, read back and compared before the client value exists, and dying with the
continuation's directory. The trade is stated rather than hidden: against a same-uid attacker the
marginal exposure is small, because the cluster CA and endpoint are already there under the same
mode, and what it buys is an EKS teardown path that authenticates at all. The wall clock's margin is
re-derived on the shipped mechanism — measured spawn plus two token reads — instead of on a
rendezvous that never occurred. One supervised child stopped existing rather than being supervised.
Focused **5/5**, primary unit **4,966/4,966**, canonical `prodbox dev check` exits 0.

**Sprint `5.46` is Done and Phase 5 recloses (2026-09-11).** Seven properties at a hundred cases
each now cover the observation-evidence scope's round trip and identity projection, in
`prodbox-unit` — the suite the policy's own tier table names, and not where the tree's only two
genuine wire round trips previously lived. The generators are the part that matters: zoned and
zoneless in roughly equal measure, same-typed fields discriminated so a swap fails rather than
passes, and no value a decoder's own default could have produced.

The mutation claim was tested rather than asserted. Dropping the zone from the wire encoder does not
compile — the field set is destructured positionally, so the abandoned binding is an unused-match
error under `-Werror`, which is Sprint `4.92`'s mechanism doing its work. Dropping the zone's value
from the identity projection while keeping its discriminator does compile, and fails the
every-field-reaches-the-projection property. Both mutations were reverted and the tree re-verified
before closing. § 3.2's own list is now honest about which of its bullets hold and which remain
table-covered. Focused **7/7**, primary unit **4,955/4,955**, canonical `prodbox dev check` exits 0.

**Sprint `5.45` is Done (2026-09-11).** All eight declared suites now have a runner.
`prodbox-haskell-style` and `prodbox-pulumi` are named by `prodbox test unit`;
`prodbox-daemon-lifecycle` by `prodbox test all`, because it spawns the built binary as a real
daemon over real sockets. The routing is exported tables rather than lists inside `case` arms, and
`testSuiteStanzaViolations` holds the declared stanzas and the routed names in bijection in both
directions, so a ninth suite cannot be added without a runner and a routed name cannot point at a
stanza nobody wrote.

Running them is what showed why it mattered, and none of it was a regression the sprint introduced.
`prodbox-haskell-style` failed on an assertion that was false about the architecture it claimed to
protect: it required the library to declare no `process` dependency, while `System.Process` supplies
the `delegate_ctlc` the streaming runner needs. `prodbox-daemon-lifecycle` failed **23 of 27** cases,
because a later sprint made the gateway daemon refuse to start without a Tier-0 deployment context
and this fixture never learned to supply one — its whole behavioural contract had been unproven
rather than merely unexercised. Both are fixed, a stale `/metrics` golden with them, and every
guarantee a governed document credited to an unrun suite is reattributed. Daemon lifecycle
**27/27**, style **17/17**, Pulumi **4/4**, primary unit **4,948/4,948**, canonical
`prodbox dev check` exits 0.

**Sprint `5.44` is Done (2026-09-11).** The canonical suite can now assert that a credential
arrived. `test/unit/CredentialDeliveryHarness.hs` re-execs the test binary as the child, reads the
credential through the kubeconfig's own `tokenFile` entry exactly as `kubectl` would, and echoes it,
so no amount of absence assertion can satisfy the case. It proves it can disagree with its subject:
against a writerless FIFO the credential does not arrive and the case fails. The elapsed-time
vocabulary is in `TestSupport` on `GHC.Clock`, which is the binding constraint — that module
compiles into five suites and two of them depend on neither `time` nor `process`, which is also why
the harness itself lives in its own module.

One thing the sprint record did not anticipate is now doctrine. A Haskell child cannot reproduce
`kubectl`'s wedge by default: GHC opens non-blocking and gets an immediate empty read, while an
ordinary C program opens blocking and waits for a writer that never comes. Both are real failures
and they are different failures, so the harness models the read mode explicitly and produces either
on demand. The negative control pins the wedge signature at **1.00 s** of a one-second bound with
the exact wall-clock refusal. Focused **5/5**, primary unit **4,943/4,943**, auxiliaries
**27/27**, **35/35**, **39/39**, canonical `prodbox dev check` exits 0.

Sprint `7.39` was no longer `Blocked` at that point: the real-child harness and the elapsed-time
assertion its counterexample is written in now existed. It landed on 2026-09-11.

**Sprint `4.94` is Done and Phase 4 recloses (2026-09-11).** `TeardownOperation` is indexed by
result as well as by cleanup surface, so an operation and its answer are tied together by
construction. The twenty catch-all arms that existed only because the type permitted an operation to
return another operation's result are deleted, and with them the one string they all collapsed into
— which is what used to discard a checkpoint interpreter's exact typed error and hand an operator a
sentence about kinds.

Three things about that sprint are worth carrying forward. The index is deliberately many-to-one,
twenty result kinds to forty operations, because a one-to-one index would have restated the
operation type rather than constraining it. Heterogeneous node lists moved to an existential whose
unpack point is exactly where the executor also holds the result, which is the whole mechanism.
And forgetting the index costs no discrimination: equality on the existential compares the operation
tag and its registered target, and that is a complete key because every surface witness has exactly
one inhabitant per surface. The binding-mismatch refusal survives unchanged, because a result index
proves the answer is the right kind and never that it belongs to this attempt.

**Sprint `4.93` is Done (2026-09-11).** Every `kubectl` in the legacy cascade's drain now runs
through the bounded runner, under a wall clock derived from the per-request bound rather than
chosen: five measured API-group discovery retries plus the resource request, plus a spawn-and-TLS
margin, forty seconds. The per-request bound is appended at one chokepoint, so no call can omit it —
seven of the nine used to. A bounded refusal is now `DrainUnobservable` rather than `DrainFailed`,
which is a real distinction: a call that did not complete is not the API server answering and
refusing. And the completion poll's five minutes is an absolute deadline read from a monotonic clock
instead of a counter decremented by the sleep interval, so the `2 + N` read-backs an iteration makes
charge their time against it; before, the documented bound was an iteration count. A wedged fake
`kubectl` is terminated at **40.04 s** and the case asserts that elapsed time, because "returned an
error eventually" cannot tell slow from wedged. Focused **4/4**, primary unit **4,939/4,939**,
canonical `prodbox dev check` exits 0.

**Sprint `4.92` is Done (2026-09-11).** `Prodbox.Lifecycle.Teardown.ScopeCodec` is the single
encoder § 2.3a required. Every durable envelope nests one canonical `ScopeWire` instead of
flattening the scope's seven fields among its own, and each bumped its own format version and
refuses older bytes rather than upgrading them — a pre-zone envelope has no zone to recover, so an
upgrade could only re-assert the absent zone that was the defect. Every digest and
canonical-identity projection derives from one field list that emits a present/absent discriminator
beside each optional value. The conversion removed about four hundred lines net, because eleven
envelopes stopped restating the same fields.

What keeps the rule rather than merely landing it: the field set is constructed by name in exactly
one function and destructured positionally by every projection, so a field added to the scope is a
missing-field error at the constructor and a constructor-arity error at each projection. Two
erasures beyond the row's own list are closed with it — `validateScopeBinding` had six clauses for a
seven-field scope and disagreed with derived `Eq` on the same two values, and `HostCleanupScope` was
a lossy in-memory projection with no zone slot, so the zone was gone before any byte was written.

canonical `prodbox dev check` exits 0.

Sprint `5.46` is no longer `Blocked`: it was blocked only on this codec existing, and its properties
